name: The denial of the existence of matter
plain_explanation: Berkeley argued there is no such thing as 'matter' existing independently of minds. What we call material objects -- trees, rocks, tables -- are really just collections ('bundles') of sensible qualities (colours, sounds, textures) that exist only insofar as they are perceived by some mind.
precise_definition: Berkeley 'maintained that material objects only exist through being perceived' (esse est percipi); the reality of sensible things 'consists in being perceived,' against the common-sense view (voiced by the character Hylas) that 'to exist is one thing, and to be perceived is another.'
why_it_mattered: This is Berkeley's most famous and radical doctrine, supported, Russell argues, by 'a number of ingenious arguments' -- though Russell contends the arguments actually establish a more modest conclusion (that we perceive only relative, mind-dependent qualities, not that all reality is mental).
historical_origin: Developed principally in The Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) and dramatized in the Dialogues of Hylas and Philonous (1713).
examples: Ronald Knox's limerick about the tree in the quad and its reply ('I am always about in the Quad... GOD')
The claim that a table is nothing but its visual shape, hardness, sound when rapped, and smell -- with no additional 'substance' behind these qualities
objections: Russell's central objection: Berkeley's arguments prove qualities are perceiver-relative, not that they are 'mental' in any well-defined sense, since Berkeley never adequately defines 'mental'
competing_positions: Common-sense/scientific realism (voiced by Hylas), which holds material substance exists independently of perception
influence_on_later_thinkers: Provoked a long line of philosophical responses and refutations; Russell notes 'to refute him has been ... a favourite pastime among metaphysicians,' foreshadowing his own treatment of Hume in the next chapter.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: God's constant perception of all things is what, for Berkeley, secures the continuous existence of the physical world -- making this a 'weighty argument,' in Berkeley's own view, for God's existence.
